series.name: The Maths Underneath
series.tagline: The mathematics behind machine learning, one idea at a time.
series.description: A fortnightly series on the mathematics that machine learning actually runs on. Each issue takes one idea, explains it in plain language, draws it, states the mathematics, and shows it running in a few lines of NumPy. No proofs, no prerequisites beyond school algebra.

issues.title: The mathematics I thought I would never use again
issues.summary: Ten years ago I set out to retrain in machine learning and found, past the notation, mathematics I already knew. Why the fundamentals outlast the frameworks, and what this series will do every fortnight.

issues.title: Your data is already geometry
issues.summary: A row of data is a point in space, and the distance between two points measures how unalike two things are. Vectors, distance, and the scaling mistake that quietly ruins it.

issues.title: Why similar means pointing the same way
issues.summary: Distance asks how far apart two points sit, which is the wrong question for taste, topic, and meaning. The dot product, cosine similarity, and the one formula behind search, recommendation, and attention.

issues.title: A matrix is a machine
issues.summary: A matrix is two things at once: a table holding a whole dataset, one example per row, and a machine that transforms every point by the same rule. One matrix multiply turns out to be a full neural-network layer, and the order of two multiplies is part of the answer.

issues.title: Running the machine backwards
issues.summary: Given a matrix and the output it produced, recover the input. Two receipts fix the price of an apple and an orange, rank measures how much information a matrix really holds, and when no exact answer exists, least squares finds the best one, which is the first machine-learning model.

series.name: The Expensive Answers
series.tagline: Architectural judgment in the AI era, one decision at a time.
series.description: A weekly series on the judgment that does not transfer to the machine: deciding what a system should be, and being able to say why. Each issue takes one architectural decision out of a working system, walks it hop by hop, and prices the tradeoff instead of declaring a winner.

issues.title: Every LLM call is a distributed transaction
issues.summary: A consultant waits 1.4 seconds for an answer. In that time her question crosses six network boundaries, races every other request in the building to update a billing counter, and streams back through every hop it came from. Why five decades of distributed systems knowledge applies in full.

issues.title: There are no wrong answers in architecture, only expensive ones
issues.summary: A board asks whether the firm should own its AI capability or rent it. The internet has a thousand confident answers, and all of them are useless without the team's context. Why architecture cannot be looked up, and the three-step method for pricing the answers available to you.

issues.title: What is the deployment quantum of an AI feature?
issues.summary: A production AI feature is four artifacts that succeed and fail together, living in four tools that ship them separately: model version, prompts, index, evaluation set. The case for one deployment unit with one version number.

issues.title: What AI coding tools leave out, with receipts
issues.summary: Four design tasks handed naively to a coding assistant, and one consistent shape in what came back: demos, with the omissions clustered exactly where production lives. The five-question review checklist, and why repairing the prompt beats blaming the tool.

issues.title: The prompt is an API contract
issues.summary: The call between deterministic code and a language model is usually treated as craft. Read it instead as the interface artifact it is: specification, test cases, schema, dependency pin, variance clause, version. Why hallucination is an unspecified failure mode, and why a vendor model upgrade is just a dependency bump, if you have contract tests to re-run.

series.name: Amplitudes
series.tagline: The linear algebra behind quantum computing, taught NumPy-first.
series.description: A series on the mathematics of quantum computing for developers who are strong in Python and light on the linear algebra. Complex numbers, state vectors, and quantum algorithms, each built in NumPy before it is shown once in Qiskit.

issues.title: Quantum computing is linear algebra you can run
issues.summary: Quantum computing looks like physics and is mostly linear algebra. A qubit in six lines of NumPy, the one rule that turns amplitudes into probabilities, and what this series will do every fortnight.

issues.title: The number system had to grow
issues.summary: Complex numbers built from one rule and read as arrows with a length and an angle. Why multiplying by e^iθ is rotation, and how a squared magnitude becomes the probability a qubit reports when measured.

issues.title: The ket is an ordinary column
issues.summary: A qubit state is a unit column of two complex numbers, and this issue builds the container: vectors, linear combinations, basis and dimension, the normalisation rule that probabilities force, and why the ket notation is a label rather than a mystery.

issues.title: A gate is a matrix
issues.summary: The verbs arrive: a quantum gate is not described by a matrix, it is one. Matrix-vector multiplication by hand, the NOT gate as a small swap, why reordering two gates changes the circuit, and the unitarity test every legal gate must pass.

series.name: Six Ideas
series.book: Six Ideas That Run the World
series.tagline: Rockets, AI, medicine and cryptography, derived from school mathematics.
series.description: A series that takes the ideas quietly running the modern world and derives them in full, using nothing beyond strong school-level mathematics. Where the real research runs past the syllabus, it says so plainly.

issues.title: Why rockets are mostly fuel
issues.summary: The Saturn V was about 93 percent propellant, and no clever engineering can change that. The rocket equation derived from school momentum, and why staging is a requirement, not a design choice.

issues.title: How your phone knows where it is
issues.summary: Your phone finds itself by timing satellite signals to a few billionths of a second, and if it ignored Einstein the blue dot would drift eleven kilometres a day. Simultaneous equations, a fourth satellite for a cheap clock, and the 1977 satellite that put relativity on a switch.

issues.title: The straight line that became AI
issues.summary: Gauss recovered the lost dwarf planet Ceres by fitting a model through imperfect observations, and his method is the direct ancestor of machine learning. Least squares derived with school calculus, a fit worked by hand, and the XOR picture that explains why deep networks are deep.

issues.title: Walking downhill in the dark
issues.summary: In 1847 Cauchy published a three-page note on solving awkward equations by walking downhill, and that note is now the engine of nearly all modern AI. The update rule run by hand, the one number that decides whether it learns or flies apart, and what changes at a hundred billion knobs. Nothing, except the arithmetic and the electricity bill.

series.name: Attention, Derived
series.tagline: The mathematics of large language models, every result derived in full.
series.description: A fortnightly series on the mathematics inside transformers and large language models. Each issue takes one result — the attention scaling factor, rotary position embeddings, KV-cache arithmetic, DPO — states it precisely, derives it in full, and shows what it costs in practice. Companion series to the book Maths for LLMs.

issues.title: Eight billion parameters, counted by hand
issues.summary: Why the first arXiv paper you open defeats you, and it is not the mathematics. The series opens by counting an eight-billion-parameter transformer by hand, down to the last norm, and reading two facts off the total that most descriptions never mention.

issues.title: In 4,096 dimensions, almost everything is perpendicular
issues.summary: Two random directions in 4,096 dimensions are all but perpendicular, and that single fact is why a transformer has room to store anything at all. The embedding lookup as a matrix product, what cosine similarity quietly discards, and the two corrections every similarity number needs.

issues.title: Why attention divides by √d
issues.summary: The most-quoted constant in the transformer, derived from a blank page: unscaled logits spread as the square root of the head width, the softmax Jacobian dies exponentially in the top-two gap, and the division exists to keep the gradient alive. Why the argument holds only at initialisation, and what QK-norm changes.

issues.title: Position is a rotation
issues.summary: Attention treats its input as an unordered set, so position must be injected, and demanding that logits depend only on relative distance forces a unique answer: rotate every query and key by an angle proportional to its position. RoPE derived from a functional equation, the wavelength ladder, and the 29 frequency pairs that never completed a turn in training.

series.name: After Shor
series.tagline: The mathematics of the post-quantum migration, one hard problem at a time.
series.description: A fortnightly series on the mathematics behind post-quantum cryptography. From modular arithmetic to lattices, Learning With Errors and the NIST standards, each issue builds one piece of the machinery replacing RSA — and prices what the migration actually asks of working engineers. Companion series to the book Maths for Post-Quantum Cryptography.

issues.title: What a quantum computer actually breaks
issues.summary: The migration deadlines are law, the standards are published, and the popular account of what a quantum computer breaks is wrong in a specific, consequential way. The accurate account, with a period you can draw and factor yourself.

issues.title: Clock arithmetic, and the one gap in it
issues.summary: The arithmetic on a clock face, done properly, is the arithmetic every operation in the post-quantum standards runs on. Where division fails and how it is repaired, why both moduli are prime, and the divisibility test that decides which transforms are even possible.

issues.title: Polynomials on the clock face
issues.summary: The standards do not compute in plain clock arithmetic but in a ring of polynomials of degree under 256 whose coefficients are clock-face numbers. Multiplication comes out as rotate-and-negate convolution, n must be a power of two, and a single divisibility check on q decides whether the ring splits all the way.

issues.title: The transform that splits the ring
issues.summary: Evaluate a polynomial at the odd powers of psi and convolution becomes pointwise multiplication: the number-theoretic transform, derived from the Chinese Remainder Theorem and checked by hand at q = 17. Splitting by square roots seven times, why ML-KEM stops at 128 quadratics while ML-DSA reaches scalars, and the thirtyfold saving the standards run on.
